The petitioners are the accused Nos.1 and 2 in CC No.1270/18 on the files of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Chalakkudy, a case instituted on a private complaint filed by the 2nd respondent alleging commission of offence under Section 420 IPC.

entities.text: Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Chalakkudy
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The allegation against the petitioners is that they had defrauded the 2nd respondent by getting a sale deed executed in respect of the property of the 2nd respondent on 31.01.2009, under the pretext that it is a lease deed.
It is the further allegation against the petitioners that, as consideration for the lease of the property, the 2nd respondent was offered allotment of shares in the company run by the petitioners.

2. The 2nd respondent lodged a private complaint before the learned Magistrate on 26.09.2018 stating that it was only on 19.06.2018 that he realised that the aforesaid document, which the petitioners managed to get executed from him, was a sale deed.

Thus, according to the 2nd respondent, the petitioners fraudulently and dishonestly induced him to believe that the document which he was made to execute on 31.01.2009, was a lease deed and that he would be allotted shares in the company of the petitioners as consideration for execution of that document.

The 2nd respondent has stated in the complaint before the learned Magistrate that he had preferred a complaint before the Mala police in connection with this incident on 09.07.2018,
but no action was initiated against the petitioners.

It is on the basis of the aforesaid contentions that the 2nd respondent approached the learned Magistrate by filing Annexure A complaint.
 3.

On 16.11.2018, the learned Magistrate passed an order in Annexure A complaint, which is extracted as follows:
 "This complaint is filed by the complainant under section 190 of Criminal Procedure Code alleging offence under section 420 of Indian Penal Code.

sentences.text: A prima facie case under section 420 of Indian Penal Code is made out in the complaint.
Hence, cognizance is taken for the said offence and taken on file as C.C.1270/18.

Issue summons to the accused on 31.12.2018"
 4.
Aggrieved by the above order of the learned Magistrate, the petitioners have preferred the present petition to quash the proceedings initiated against them.

5. Heard the learned counsel for the petitioners, the learned counsel for the 2nd respondent and the learned Public Prosecutor representing the 1st respondent.
6.

The learned counsel for the petitioners contended that there is 2025:KER:10210 absolutely no justification for the inordinate delay in preferring a complaint in respect of the alleged fraudulent act of the petitioners misrepresenting the 2nd respondent about the nature of the document which he was made to execute on 31.01.2009.

It is further argued by the learned counsel for the petitioners that the above said document, a copy of which is produced as Annexure C, is a registered sale deed, and hence, the normal presumption under Section 114 (illustration e) is that it has been executed in the due course.

According to the learned counsel for the petitioners, there is absolutely no justification for the failure of the 2nd respondent to challenge Annexure C sale deed by instituting a civil suit, if he was bonafidely aggrieved by the alleged misrepresentation, which resulted in the execution of the above document.
It is also pointed out by the learned counsel for the petitioners that the learned Magistrate had passed the impugned order in a mechanical manner without applying his judicial mind into the matter.

7. The learned counsel for the 2nd respondent contended that the failure of the 2nd respondent to prefer complaint against Annexure C, sale deed, for a period of more than 9 years, was only due to the faith he had reposed upon the petitioners, with whom, he had worked abroad for several years.

According to the learned counsel for the 2nd respondent, the 2nd 2025:KER:10210 respondent approached the authorities concerned, immediately after he realised the fraud perpetrated upon him by the petitioners.
Thus, it is argued that the issue involved in this case is not a matter which could be interfered with, in a proceeding under Section 482 Cr.P.C, by this Court.

8. As already stated above, the challenge in this proceedings is mainly against the order passed by the Judicial First Class Magistrate, Chalakkudy, on 16.11.2018, taking cognizance of the offence alleged in the private complaint filed by the 2nd respondent.

A reading of the aforesaid order, which is extracted hereinabove, would show that there is absolutely nothing stated thereunder as to whether the sworn statement of the complainant and witnesses were recorded, and the court applied its mind over the materials on record in such enquiry for getting satisfied as to whether,
there are sufficient grounds to proceed against the petitioners.

Instead, what has been stated in the aforesaid order is a mere superficial remark that a prima facie case Jose Thomas Pattara vs State Of Kerala on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99363391/
3 under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is made out in the complaint, and hence,
cognizance is taken for the said offence.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: That is not the way in which a Magistrate is expected to act, while taking cognizance of the offence on the basis of a complaint instituted by a person.

It is true that the order taking cognizance of the offence and issuing process to the accused need not contain a detailed analysis of the 2025:KER:10210 averments in the complaint, and the evidence submitted by the complainant in support of the same.

But, at the same time, the Jurisdictional Magistrate is expected to mention, though briefly, in the order, about the reason why he arrived at the finding that there are sufficient grounds to proceed against the accused.

As far as Annexure B order is concerned, it is not possible to discern whether the learned Magistrate had recorded the sworn statement of the complainant or any other witness before arriving at the finding that a prima facie case under Section 420 IPC is made out.

As rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the petitioners, the Apex Court has held time and again that the issuance of process against the accused is not an empty formality, and the Magistrate is required to apply his mind as to whether sufficient ground for proceeding exists in the case or not, and that the formation of such an opinion is required to be stated in the order itself.

In Lalankumar Singh and Others vs. State of Maharashtra [(2022)SCC Online SC 1383],
the Apex Court has held that the order is liable to be set aside, if no reasons are given therein while coming to the conclusion that there is a prima facie case against the accused.

Central Bureau of Investigation [(2015) 4 SCC 609], Mehmood Ul Rahman v. Khazir 2025:KER:10210 Mohammed Tunda [(2015) 12 SCC 420] and Krishnalal Chawla and Others vs. State of Uttarpradesh and another [(2021) 5 SCC 435].

sentences.text: Annexure B order passed by the learned Magistrate is against the law laid down by the Apex Court in the aforesaid decisions.
Therefore, I am of the view that the aforesaid order passed by the learned Magistrate is liable to be set aside.

However, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that the matter is to be reconsidered by the learned Magistrate, who shall apply his judicial mind on the materials placed before him, and pass an order as to whether there are sufficient grounds to proceed against the petitioners.

In any case, if there had been omission on the part of the learned Magistrate to record the statement of the complainant at least, before proceeding to the stage of Section 204 Cr.P.C, an opportunity has to be provided to the complainant and witnesses, if any, to tender sworn statements before the Magistrate.

Accordingly, the present petition is disposed of as follows:
1) The order dated 16.11.2018 of the Judicial First Class Magistrate, Chalakkudy, in Crl.M.P No.8025/2018 in CC No.1270/2018 is hereby set aside.
2) The case is remanded back to the learned Magistrate for fresh consideration from the stage when the 2025:KER:10210 learned Magistrate admitted Annexure A Jose Thomas Pattara vs State Of Kerala on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99363391/

4) After completion of such enquiry under Section 200 and 202 Cr.P.C, as the case may be, the learned Magistrate shall pass an order which should reflect the reasons why he arrived at the finding thereunder, whether it be one issuing process to the accused or dismissing the complaint under Section 203 Cr.P.C.
